notes: Many boroughs and cities levy local sales taxes, with their own exemptions (some exempt groceries); treated here as applying to every category unless the local rate table says otherwise.
gaps: Excursion Inlet (Haines Borough) is not a Census place; its 2.5% (4.5% in summer) is left out

Alaska has no state sales tax. The boroughs and cities that belong to the Remote Seller Sales Tax Commission are taken from its rate sheet; cities that tax sales but haven't joined are taken from the state's Alaska Taxable 2025 report (Table 1B). Anchorage, Fairbanks and most of the state have no general sales tax.
Kenai Peninsula Borough: the sheet lists its 3% (and Homer's) with a June-August season, which applies to groceries (taxed only in summer); the 3% general rate is used year-round.
Seasonal rates: the October (winter) rate is used; summer rates are higher in several places (see notes).
Some Alaska cities cap the taxable amount per item or transaction (e.g. Homer at $500); not modeled.

Gasoline: many Alaska communities are off the road system, so residents can't drive to another town for fuel. A low gasoline retention there reflects how local fuel sales are counted (gas stations' jobs, and other stores' fuel sales by the national mix of what they sell), not fuel bought elsewhere, and the sales tax shown on gasoline that leaves is not tax lost to another town. In Juneau, for example, part of the gasoline is sold by a warehouse club and a general merchandise store (Costco and Fred Meyer), which are counted by their store type's national mix, in which fuel is a few percent of sales, so Juneau's low gasoline retention partly reflects how those sales are counted.

Taxes on alcohol and tobacco come from the state's Alaska Taxable 2025 report (Office of the State Assessor, Table 1B, rates as each municipality reported them): percent-of-sale taxes are counted in the alcohol and tobacco rates; per-unit and wholesale tobacco taxes are excises and are left out, as are bed, car rental and marijuana taxes. Table 1B also gives the sales taxes of 52 cities that aren't on the remote-seller sheet; they are counted from it (some as last reported for 2022 to 2024). Where both sources give a rate and they differ, the newer remote-seller sheet is used and the difference is noted.

warn: Bethel is the largest hub for the 56 remote communities of the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta, none of them on the state's highway system (Alaska DOT&PF, Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta Transportation Plan), so its stores also sell to people from the villages around it. Its prices are also far above the national level at which residents' spending is measured here: the University of Alaska Fairbanks Food Cost Survey (September 2018) put a week's food for a family of four in Bethel at about 2.6 times the US average. Both raise Bethel's store sales per household and its pull factors, so read them as a high-priced regional center's.

Kusilvak Census Area's villages are off the road system, and fuel and goods there cost far more than the national prices at which residents' spending is measured here, which raises its pull factors, gasoline's most of all.
